0012.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Vers.1.

body.t: Moreover Job continuid his Parable.
Why doth Job call what he had to say a Parable? The Origi¬
nal word signifies to rule, to govern, to govern as a Prince,
para-whose righteous Precepts and Commands, whose Lawes and
son-Counsels, his people ougnt to obey: Speeches or Sentences which
are full of wisdom and of truth are called Parables for a threefold
Fcason.
First, Because Parables and wise Sentences rule over the spirits
of men, as Princes and Magistrates do over their bodies or out¬
ward man. Parables carry so convincing a light, so great an autho¬
rity in them, that every mans Judgment and understanding sub¬
mits and falls down before them, such words bear rule and
sway. And though many contradict truth, & rebel against it, yet
truth will subdue, even them to its pouer, who would not submit
toits rule, nor bow to its Scepter. And Tob might well call what
he had to say, a Parable, a collection of ruling sentences, seeing
the issue his friends, who were no friends to what he said, were
forced to yield themselves up to it, and submit to him by the final
sentence or determination of God himself.
Secondly, Parables are so called, because such speeches came
usually from the mouths of Princes and great Persons; they were
speeches of Rulers, therefore ruling speeches. Solomon spake pro¬
verbs of Parables, who was a great King, and ruled over men
more by wisdome than he did by power.
Thirdly, Because whether men will submit to such speeches
and truths or no, yet their Judgments, actions and opinions must
be tryed and ruled by them. Parables are touchstones of truth,
they are rules, and therefore ought to rule.
Again, Others derive the Oiginal word which we rendet a Pa¬
rable, from a root which signifies to liken, or to make like; this also
suits uell with the nature of Parables, which are usually expressed
by Similes or Similitudes, compiring one thing with another, or
para-one thing to another (Math. 13.3.) At that time Jesus spake
unto them many things in Parables. We have seaven distinct Pari¬
bles in that Chapter; and what were those Parables? they were
all Similitudes; A Sower went out to sow; There you have a Pa¬
rable, intimating all sorts of Gospel-Hearers, by four sorts
ground. Therc also you have che Parable of the grain of Mustard¬

0013.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOR. Vers.

body.t: seed, &c. holding forth the growing power of Grace. It is said
of Abrabam, that by faith he offered up Isaac, accounting that God
vas able to raise him from the dead, from whence also be receivid
bim in a figure, or parable (Heb. 11. 19.) There was an Image
or Similitude of death upon Abrabam, in reference to that bles¬
sing; his own body was dead, and Sarah was dead too as to child¬
bearing: But he considering those deaths out of which he had his
son, was willing to offer his son to death when God called him to
it, because he knew God was able to raise him even from the
dead, from whence he at first receïved him in a figure. And
we expound Abrabams receiving of Isaac from the dead, not of
his first receiving him from his owne and Sarabs dead body, but of
his second receiving him, after he at Gods command had bound
him upon the Altar, ready to be slaine and offered up in sacrifice,
mikes no difference as to the poynt in hand; Thit being also
an illustrious parable, or figure of death, and of a resurrection
from it.
Again, parables are called Similitudes or Similyes, because
they resemble, and beare (is it were) the express Image of their
wisdome, gravity, modesty, and truth, who spake and held them
forth. All words are or fhould be the Image of the mind, and
Parables are a beautiful Image of the beautiful mind. A para¬
ble is taken four wayes in Scripture.
First, for any Divine Mixime, Axiom, or Principle, which
generally obtaineth and is retained among all sorts ot meq,
(Pro. 26. 7.) As the feet of the lame are not equall, sois a Para-
ble in the mouth of a fool; that is, a Divine holy sentence, a grave
and wise sentence, is an uncomely thing in the mouth of a wicked
man. A Parable in his mouth is like a Pearle in a swines snout.
Secondly, A Parable is a dark and a hard saying: they said
unto Christ now speakest thou plainly, and doest not speak a Para-
ble. A Parable is there opposed to i plain speech; there is an
outward darknesse of words incompassing that light; and hence
Parable and a dark saying are put together, as expressing eich
t’other. (Psal.49.4.) I mill encline mine eare unto a Parable, and O-
pen my darke saying upon the harpe; the darke saying in the latter
part, is the parable in the former part. So (Psal. 78.2.) Imill
open my mouth in a Parable, I mill utter darke sayings of old.
Parable is a kind of a riddie, or as we may veil expresse it, a Pa-

Thirdly, Any similitude or resemblances from things in hea¬
ven or things on carth, is a parable.
Fourthly, A mans judgment or opinion, in any case is his
parable: every mans opinion, whether true or false, is a pirable
him, and he would have it so to others, that is, he would have
a ruling sentence. Thus Mr Broughton translites this text, and
Tob proceeded to continut his oration; and another, Tob proceuded
deliver his opinion; so that a mans opinion or sentence (be it what
will) is his parable, or that which rules him, and which he de¬
fires may rule all others. Most men would have every Sheafe bon
to theirs; and some have a higher ambition to mike the minds
and judgements of men stoop to them, than ever any had to make
the bodyes of men stoope to them: They would have every opi¬
nion of theirs a parable, like a Prince upon the throne, giving the
law or rule to others. So much for the nature and extent of the
word, by which Job expresseth all that he had to say, A parable.

esteemed of God, are an abomination in the sight of men.
These sufferings of the Saints in their owne credit, or in the opi¬
nbn of men, serve the holy ends and purposes of God, as much
any of their sufferings, whether in body or state, by the oppressions
and persecutions of men. And therefore Saints are detained under
these tryalls as well as any other, till those holy ends are served;
and longer than that, they shall not be detained under them. This
tongue-rod either of wicked men, or of mistaken and misunder¬
standing brethren, ssall not rest upon the lot of ths righteous;

0028.head: Chap.27. An Exposition apon the Bok of JOB. Verf. 2.

body.t: Though God take away their Judgment for the present, yet at
lasthe will give judgment sor them. David was not onely risen
up to that assurançe, but had it in experience (Psal. 9. 3,4,5.
uhen mine enemies are turned back, they shall fall and perist at
thy presence; for thou hast maintained my right, and my cause, thou
sattest in the tbrone judging right, or in righteousnesse. David found
God standing np presently for him, and asserting his innocency,
he found God sitting in his throne, and giving right judgment
against his enemy. But is notGod alwayes upon his thronc ?or doth
he any thing at any time upon his throne but whit is right? Woe
tothose who thinke otheruise; God is alwayes upon his throne,
and can doe nothing but right there. But he doth not alwayes give
out, or declare his righteous judgments, or the righteousnesse of
his judgments; All men have not the fruit or benefit of them, as
David then had. Thou hast rebuked the heathen, thou hast destroyed
the wiched, thou hast put out their name for ever and ever. Thus the
Lord did execute Judgment for David even upon the place:
He gives a like report of the present appearance ot God for him
Pial. 41. 12. )As for me thou upholdest me in mine integritie;
that is, while I walk uprighrly, sincerely, and with a single heart
thou takest my part, and maintainest me against all mine enemies,
or notwichstanding the oppesitien of mine enemies, thou. doest
maintaine in me a defite and purpose to walke still sincerely, up¬
rightly, and inthe singleness of my heart. And indeed we have
great reason to hold fast, and to hold on in our integrity, while the
Lord undettake’s to uphold us in our integricy. And it he should
let us fall in our integrity, or our integrity fall for a while, yet we
have a promise (Psal. 37. 6.) that the Lord will doe it for all his
people at last, or in the fittest season. waite upon the Lord, trust
also in him, and he shall bring it to passe; he shall bring forth thy
righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noone day. Though
thy judgment or right be like midnight, darke, and obscure, so
that none can see it; though the Lord himselfe ( as Job here
speakes ) seemeth to have taken away thy Judgment, yet waite a
while, and thou shalt see a glorious turne, thou shalt see darkness
turned to light, and midnight to noone day; thou shalt see God
bringing forth thy righteousnesse as the licht, and bringing back or
restoring thy judgment (which he tooke away) like unto the noone¬
day. Thus Paul comfortedhimfelse when God had taken away

0029.head: Chap,27. An Exposition npon the Bork of JOB. Verf,2.

body.t: his judgment, and he lay under the severest judgment of men,
(1. Cor. 3.4,5, 6.) Mith me it is a very small thing that I should
be Judģed of you, or of mans Judgment (I know men censure me li¬
beraliy) for I know nothing ey my selfe ( I am cleare in my owne
conscience) yet I am not hereby Justified, But he that Judgeth
me is the Lord. God judgeth all men presently, as to his owne
knouledg of their estate, and he will ere long publish the know¬
ledge ot their state to others, even in the eares and tothe open
view of all. Therefore (the Apostle concludes, v. 5.) Judg no¬
thing before the time untill the Lord come, who both will bring
light the hidden things of darbness, and mill manifest the counsels ot
the heart: and then shall every man (who hath been falsely accused
and wrongfully difgraced by men ) have praise of God. In the
Great Judgment God will take away that Judgment of outward
approbation from all wicked men which the world had given
them, & he will give that Judgment of outward approbation to all
godly men, which himselse had taken away from them while the
were in this world;and they shall say in that day, The Lord liveth
who hath restored our Judgment, which he was pleased (as Job
saithhere) once to take away.
And the almighry wbo hath veved my foule.
Here againe we are to repeate orsuppose the oath, At God li-
veth, who hath taben anay my judgment, and (as) the Almighty
liveth) mho hath vexed my soul. This title of God almight),
notes, first, the strength; secondly, the goodnesse of God. As the
Lord is powerfull, so he is the spring, and fountaine of goodnesse
tand mercy to his people; neverthelels though the Lord be thus al¬
emight y, though he be thus mercifull, and good in himself, yet (saith
(fob) he vexeth my soul. The text is, He maheth my soule bitter,
He is bitter to me, it is usual to expresse affliction by bitternesse,
and the inflicting of affliction upon any, by imbittering them.
There is a threefold notion of bittetnesse in Sctipture, First, Sin
is called bitternesse ( Hos. 12.14.) Epbraim provobed him to anger
most bitterty. We translate in the superlative; the text is, Ephraim
provoked him to anger mith bitternisses. What provokes God
anger ? it is sin; and what is sin? bitternesse, yea bittetnesses;there
is a collection of all bitternesses in any sin; how many bitternes¬
fes are there then ina collection of many fins! Epbraim provoted

0030.head: Chap.27. An Expoifition upon the Book of JOR. Verf.2.

body.t: him to anger with bitternesses, that is, with many sins. We tendet
well, Ephraim provoked him to anger most bitterly; either imply¬
ing the degree of Ephraims sinfulness, which provoked God to
anger, his was a high provocition, or implying the degree of that
anger which the Lord expressed by reason of that provocation;
The Lord was most bitterly angry at the sinfull provocations of
Ephraim. And this complyes with the following notion of Bitterr
ness in Scripture.
Secondly, Anger, and wrath it selfe is called bitternesse, or
bitter thing; anger is hot, and heate makes the naturall humour
bitter; whence by allusion anger is expressed by bitternesse, be¬
cause it doth imbitter the spirit, as much heate imbittereth the
stomacke. The word is used in that prophesie of the Ram, and the
He-goat (Din. 8. 8.) And I saw him (that is, the He-goite) come
close to the Ram, and he was moved with choller against him ; so we
translite; the text is (’tis the word here ufed in Job) he was im¬
hittered against him, or vexed at him. The Goate (or Ale xander
King of Grecce) was imbittered against the Ram (or against Da¬
rius the King of Persia ) and smote the Ram, and brabe his tmo
hornes. Solomen saith (Pro. 17. 11.)! An evill man secketh only
rebellion; some read it, He secheth onely anger; The text is, An
evil man secketh onely bitternesse, that is, to imbitter the spirits of
others; he careth not how much anger he kindles among men,
and therefore he loves to blow the coales. Whereas it is the bu¬
siness of a gracious man to sweeten, and quiet the spitits ef others.
He is peaceable himselfe to others, and a peace-miker between
others; But an evil man sec keth onely anger.
Thirdly, Bitternesse is put for affliction. That which makes
our lives bitter tous, may well be called bitterness. When that
good woman Naomi came home, afflicted, and emptied, to
her freinds and fellow Citizens, who had formerly knowne her,
they being much moved between compassion and wonder at her
sad condition, said, is this Naomi! Is it possible; What is this
Naomi! Then she said unto them (Rath. 1. 20 ) Call me not
Naomi ( that is, beautifull ) but call me Marah, ( that is, bitter)
for the Almiçhty hath dealt very bitterly with me: I ment out full,
and the Lord hath brougbt me home emptie. And is bitterness is put
for worldly forrow, or for that forrow which ariseth from trou¬
bles or vants in the thinss oftue vorld : so also for Seicitallo¬

0031.head: Chap.27. An Exposition npon the Bosk of JOR. Verf.2,

body.t: Godly sorrow. (Lech. 12. 10.) They shall look upon me whom
they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mournethfor
bis only Son, and they shall be in bitternesse for him, as one that is
bitterness for his first-born. That which the Prophet calls maurn¬
ing in the former part of the verle, he calls being in bitterness in the
latter; As it is an evil and a bitter thing to sin against God,
sinning against God should be followed with that good, but bitter
thing, mourning or godly sorrow. Here Job was vexed or im¬
bittered, not so much withisorrou for his sins, as with the sence
of Gods afflicting hand in the tryal of his graces. Thus the Al¬
migbty ( saith he) hath vexad my soul.
He did not say, the almighty had vexed bis body or estate, though
the Lord did vex both, or him in both; He pitched only upon
the vexation of his soul; His affliction went deep, it reached not
only his skin and flesh, but his soul and spirit; yet when he saith,
The Almighty hath vexel my soul, he doth not meane it of
soul-affliction, either alone, or in opposition to the afflictions ot
the body, such as are trouble of mind for sin, disquietness of con¬
science, and sence of divine wrath, but he means thus much only
(I suppose) in this place, That his troubles were great and but¬
densome, so greit and burdensome, that he wis smitten all over,
and felt the sad effects of the Lords afflicting hand in the grief of
his soule, as well as in the pains of his body. The Almighty hath
vextd my soul.
Observe;
Firft, The Lord hatb allponer in his hand.
He were not Almighty, if he had not.Some men have presumed
themselves able to do all things, and so have most blasphemously
usurped this attribute of almightinesse, but none ever were so.
Secondly, Observe;
Itis not for want of poer that God doth not pres ently relieve
and belp his distressed servants.
As God never wants strength to afflict, so not to deliver. He i
alwayes furnished with power to execute whatsoever he hath
will to appoynt. When we lye in iffliction unrelieved, we are
more ready to question the power of God, than our own sinful¬
oess. The femes had such apprehensions et God, is ve may collect
I

0032.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bock of JO». Versea.

body.t: from that redargution in the prophet (Isa. 59.1.) The Lerdi
hand is not shortned that it cannot saue; As if he had said, ye thinke
ye are ina distresse so deepe that the Lords hand is not long e¬
nough now (though it have been heretofore) to reach your sal¬
vation, whereas in truth the Lords hand is not shortned thit it
cannot save: The reason why ye are not delivered, is not beciuse
God hath not power to deliver you, but because your sins stand
the way of your deliverance. Tour iniquities have separated be¬
tmeen yon and yourGod, and your sins have hid his face from you that
he mill not heare. Till our sins be removed either by pardon or re¬
pentance, or both, troubles will not remove from us. While the
fountaine of goodis separated from us, evill must needs abide with
us. Our helpe is alwayes in the haud of God, but he hath not al¬
wayes awill to helpe us, and the most usual reason why his will
not to sive or deliver us from or out of trouble, is because our
vill is so big with fin, and so much in the deliverance of it.
Thirdly, observe;
The Lord is sometimes se farr from putting ferth his powir
releive his precious oues, that he puts it forth to afflict and
lay them low.
To comfort the soulis the most proper worke of God, and yet
tis his work also to vex the soule. And as he speaks to the wicked
his wrath and vexeth them in his sore displeasure (Psal.2.5.)
so’tis his pleasure (yet not without infinite wisdom and gracious
intendments also) tospeak to many who are Godly in his anger,
and to vexe their soules under the severest dispensations.
Fourchly, Observe,
Affictions are to the soule as bitter thingi to the tast.
No chastning for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous,
(Heb. 12. 11.) Though affliction bring forth peaceable fruits of
righteousnesse to them thit are exercised thereby, yet to be under
that exercise is sorrow and trouble; Even those chastnings which
are (as to the isfue) onely for the tryall and cleansing of the soul,
are also (in the way) a vexition tothe soul.
Fifthly, Observe;
Saints ackvowledge the hand of God in all their afflictions.
Thealmigbiy hath vexed my soule, faith fab. He had many o¬

0033.head: Chap.27. An Exposstion upon the Bok f JOR. Vers.2.

body.t: ther hands upon him, but he tooke most notice of the hand of
God, as hath been shewed at the 21. verse of the first Chapter,
and else-where in this Book. Faith seeth him who is invisible,
vexing as well as comforting; And ’tis comfort to Saints, not only
to remember God in their afflictions, but to remember that it
God who afflicts them.
Sixthly Note;
A godly man hath good thoughts of God, while he ascribes bis pe¬
nall evills or sufferings unto God.
Tob gnew and acknowledged that God was not onely good in
himselfe, but good to him while he vexed his soul;while God af¬
flictsus and mikes us poore, or sick, while he strips us naked of
riches, children, friends and relations, yet we should say (as Da¬
vid, (Plal. 73. 1.) Traly God is good to Irael, even to all them
that are upright in heart. While the Lord vexeth our souls, our
soules should magnifie the Lord. While the Lo.d makes our souls
bitter, our souls should sweeten the dealings of God, While the
Lord troubles us we should not be displeased, yea we should be
well-pleased with the Lord. God doth his people no hurt, much
lesse doth he intend them hurt when he makes them smart; There¬
fore it is their dutie, even when they smart, to make the fairest re¬
ports of him to all that come about them. God is such a fountaine
sends forth both bitter waters & sweet, as to our present sence,
but all the waters which he sends forth are sweete as to our future
benefit; therefore though sense say of some of them they are bit¬
ter, yet let faith say of all of them they are sweet.
Seventhly, Observe;
Saints afflictions are often very deepe afflictions.
They goe donne to the very foul. Not only vere Tosephs feite
Burt in the stocks, but the iron entred into his soule, as the old tran¬
slation hathit (Psal.105. 18.) or, as ue put in the Margin, his
soule came into iron ; thit is, he was afflicted, or (as Job here
speaks) vexed to his soule. As the word of God (Heb. 4. 2.)
pierceth to the dividing, so the rod of God can peïrce to the grie¬
ving and paining of soule ind spirit, of the joynts and marrow.
Thus Job deciphers God in his dealing with him; As God liveth,
who hath taten away my Tadgment, and the almighty who hath vex¬

0034.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bok ef Jo». Vers.3

body.t: my soule; But what was fobs oath or whether did it teud? the
two next verses shew us, First, the continuance of this oath upon
him: secondly, the concernment of ir,or about what he tooke this
solemne oath. The former we have in the third verse, the latter
the fourth.
Verf. 3. All tbe mbile my breatb is in mi, and thi spirit of Guod
is in my nostrills, (v.A.) My lips shall not speake wic¬
Rdnesse, nor my tongue utter deceit.
Job takes his oath, not for a diyor a yeare, but for his lite, all
the while my breath is in me, that is, as long as I live. While breath
continues, life continues. It is said (Gen. 2. 7.) The Lord brea¬
thed into man the breath of life. The hebrew word for breatb hath
an affinity with chat by which the heivens ire expressed in the
sime languige; implying (say some) that the breath of man cime
from heaven, or was of God; The breith of man wis not creited
with man in the forming of the body, as it was with the beists;
but after the body wis formed God infused the breath, and there¬
fore Moses in that text fperkes distinctly concerning man; First,
The Lord God formed man out of the dust of the carth, & (then)brea¬
thed inte his nostrills the breath of life, and man bicame a living
soult. So then, To have breath in us, is to have life in us, or it isa
circumlocution of life, ind as soone as breath departs life departs,
we dye. It is said (1 Kings 17. 17.) That the Son of the Wo¬
min, the Mistresse of the house, fell sick, and his sicknesse was so
sore that there mas no breath lest in bim, thit is, he dyed. When Eu¬
tychus falling from the third loft mas taken up dead, Paul went
downe and fell on him, and imbraeing bim said, trouble not yeur
selves for his life is in him. The Grecke is, His soule is in him.
They who tooke him up concluded him dead, because he did not
breath, kuowing that when breath goes, life goes too; But Paul
fercht him againe by prayer, and his breath returned. When Paul
embraced him, breath re-entred him; And therefore he saith be¬
remptorily his life is in him, either because it was then returned,
or beciuse he knew it would; according to the usuil language
faith he spi ke of it, as of a thing already done. Sence and reason
said, he was dead, because his breath was gone; but faith said his
life was in him, knowing that God was able to bring the breath
back againe. Mans lise amounts cnly to this, He hath his breatb

0035.head: Chap. 27. An Expofition upon the Bok of JOR. Verf.3.

body.t: his nostrils. (Isa. 2. 22.) Or (as Tob speakes )breath is in him.
All the mhile my breath is in me,
And the spirit of God in my nastrils.
This latter clause is of the same signification with the former,
and is but a repetition in other words, yet there is som difference
of opmion, whit fhould be here meant by the Spirit of God.
There are among the ancients who understind, the holy Spirit,
not only the Spirit ot God,but God the Spirit. And they tell us,
That we have a description or specificition of the whole Trinity
this Text; By the living God, understanding the Father, and by the
almighty, the Sonne, and by the Spirit of God, the Holy Ghost. But
cannot comply with this interpretition; For though I doubt not
but Tob had the Spirit of God, yet here he is describing his natu¬
rall life, not his spiritual; And it is plaine that he intends nothing
but his naturall life by the Spirit of God, because he calleth it the
Spirit of God in his nostrils. Tne holy sanctifying, comforting Spi¬
rit, is not said to be a Spirit in our nostrils; that’s no way suitable
to Scripture-speaking, which saith, That the Holy Spirit of God
dwels in our hearts, or in our inner man, as also in our bodyes, but
never in our nostrils. So then Spirit is the same with breath. As
for that addition, The Spirit of God, it signifieth only thus much,
that God is the maker or author of the Spirit here spoken of, not
thit the Spirit here spoken of is God our maker; orthit God is the
efficient cause of this Spirit, as of all other creatures, not that this
Spirit is God by nature. So thit when Tob saith, Al the while my
breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nestrils, his scope is,
to give utmost assurance to his friends, that he intended to hold his
owne to the urmost. His breath he granted might quickly pisse
away, and the Spirit in his nostrils sit upon his lips ready to take
leive and be gone; but if his life should continue long, and he
appeare rather like a Home-dweller than a stranger or sojourner
in this world, yet he was fully purposed to abide and continue in
the same opinion and defence of himselfe unto the end.
Hence Observe;
First, Life is ef God.
The Spirit whereby we live the life of niture, as well is the Spi¬
rit whereby ve live the life of Grace, che Spirit in our nostills as

0036.head: Chap.27. An Expofition upon the Book OT JOE. Verf. 3.

body.t: wellas the Spirit in our hearts is the gift, the onely gift of God;
all the powers in heaven and earth ( without God) cannot give
breath, nor make life. Art hath imitated living things, but never
was there any artist which couldemake things live; the Painter can
make the image of a mau, but he cannot put life into his image,
God onely doth that.
First, Then our life depends upon God, we live or dye at his
pleasure. ( Psal. 104. 29.) Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled;
thou takest amay their breath, they dye and returne to their dust.
Life is breath given, death is breath taken away. Dantel tells Ne¬
buchadnez zar, TheG̃od in mhose hand thy breath is, and mhose are all
thy wayes, hast thou not honoured (Chap, s. 23.) He describeth
God in his Greatnesse by having that Great Kings breath in his
hand, that is, in his power ; He gave it thee, and he can tike
from thee when he will. David puts this power among those Ex¬
cellencies of God for which he is to be magnified by mankinde
Psal. 66. 8, 9.) O blesse our God, ye people, and mabe the voyct of
his praist to be heard, mhich holdith our soule in life. The Hebrew
(as our Margin hath it )is, which putteth our soul in life. We miy
cake in both readings, and not at all enlarge the text beyond its
due bounds, for God first putteth our soule in life, that is, he cau¬
seth our soule, that is, our selves or our persons to live by bringing
and uniting soule and body together. Secondty, He holdeth our
soule in life, by preserving or delivering us from those daily dan¬
gers and evils which threaten to separate or divorce our soules
from our bodyes. It God did not hold and keepe our soules in
life, our soules could not continue in life one minute. No sooner
doth the living God withdraw his hand of preservation, but man
among the dead, or upon the borders of dissolution; diseases
and dangers would soone breake this union, and unty this marri¬
age-knot between soule and body, if God did not hold it: when
God lets goe his hold, out it goes, when God calleth, out it must.
As God said to Abrahan- Gen.12.1.) Get thee out of thy Coun¬
tri, and from thy hindred, and from thy fathers house; God called
him from his owne home, and he willingly obeyed; So when God
calles our spirit out of the body, and commands it to dislodge,
must dislodge and come out whether we will or no. And secing
our life or breath depends upon God, and a call ftom him fetch¬
eth it forth at any time, let us pray ( to speske in alluf̃ion to that

0037.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOB. Vers.3.

body.t: of Christ in the Gospel about the miseries thit were to come up¬
on Terusalem, let us (I say ) pray ) that the flight of it may not be
the winter of sin, in the night of ignorance, or on the Siboith,
(I meane Satans Saboath) of carnal security and impenitency.
Seeing our breath must depart when God calls, it is our wisdome
to mike ready for our departure. It is best to be ready and pre¬
pared for that which we cannot avoid, how uuready and un-pre¬
pired soever we are. Most live as if their life were in their owne
band or at their oun dispose, & not in the hind or dispose of God.
They who live as they list, seem to say, they can live as long as they
list. Let us remember, that as we are daily dying, and that as
cannot be many dayes before we must die, so we may die any day.
As it is appoynted for all men once to dye by a general decree,
soit is appoynted by a speciall decree when every man must dye.
This decree is in the breast ot God, in whose hand our breath is.
Therefore as the Prophet exhorts (Zeph. 2. 1, 2.) let us gather
our selves togcher, yea gither together (in the icting of faith
and every grace) before the decree bring forth, for our gathering
our fathers in the Grave.
Secondly, Obferve;
Our life is but breath in our nostrills.
Such is the frailty of mans lise, that his life stands alwayes atthe
doore, as if it were taking leive of him. How soone may that be
gone, which cinnot stay when our breath is gone? When the Holy
Ghost would shew how poore a thing man is, and how little or
rather how not at all to be trusted, or reckoned upon, He saith,
Cease ye from man, whose breath ùs in his nostrills (Ifa. 2. 22.)As
thit were the most disparaging expression of mans life. Why
should we keepe so much adoe about any man living, seeing his
breath, and so his life, may be gone before he or we can doc any
thing. And as the Prophet calleth us off from relyince upon man
upon the same reason calleth us off from relyance upon great men
speciall, knowing how apt we are to rely upon them, and to
give the Gods of the earth that honour which is due onely to the
God of heaven, (Psal. 146.4, 5.) Put not jour trust in Prirces,
nor in the son of man, in mhom there is no helpe; his breath goeth
ferth, he returnes to dest, in that very day his ihoughis perisp.

0038.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Vert-;

body.t: unlesse breath goe forth we dye, and death is nothing else but the
going forth of the breath. Life is the going forth ot the breath
by respiration, and death is the going forth of the breath by ex¬
spiration. And howsoone may respiring be changed into exspi¬
ring ? And as we dye when our breath goes out but returnes not,
when it cannot get out. The body hath been called the prison
the soul, and so in fome sence it is; but here is a riddle, The keep¬
ing of the prisoner is quite contrary to that of other prisoners;
we keep prisoners by shuttingup the doores, but if you shut up
the doores of your body, the mouth and nostrils, you loose your
prisoner, the soul gets presently out : Hlalesse the breath have li¬
bertie to pisse eut, you cannot hold it. The way to kecpe the
breath in, is to give it free passage out; if the outward ayre be
kept out, and the breath kept in, life is lost, and we know how
fmall amatter will doe this; A gnat, a fly, the stone of a Raison,
fingle haire have done it in great eximples. Therefore let us
cease from other men, but chiefly from our selvs, seing we & they
are so soone ceasing: let us not over rate the persons of other men,
nor (which we are very apt to doe) our own, for our breath is
our Nostrills. Thus Tob describes himselfe in his mortal stite,
Al the wbile my breatb is in me, and the Spirit of God in my no¬
strils; As if he had said, This is the short and the long, the all
of my resolutions, while I am in this world, that whether my
life or stiy in this world be long or short, I am strongly resolved,
That
Verf. 4. My lips shall not speabe michednesse, nor my tongueutte¬
deceit.
In this verse Tob removes tuo evils or diseases, or two evill dis¬
eases of the tongue from himselfe, First, the speaking of miched¬
nesse, which is openly evñl; Secondiy, the speaking of deceit, which
closely evill. These two are joyned as in the text, so (Psa, 10.
7.) His ( that is, the wicked mans) mouth is full of cursing deceit
and fraud : from both these instruments and engines of the

Though he hath gained.

Wben God tabetb amay bis soule?
There are tuo readings of this last clause.
First, Some derive the word, which we translite, tabeth away,

mbat is the hope of the hypocrite, though he hath gained, and God

Some get much, but their souls never rest, they are tumbled up

wbat hath a man of all his labour, and of the vexation of bis beart,

My Spirit mas grieved mithin me (Chap. 7. 15. ) The Chaldee

body.t: First, A wicked man while he liveth may be fall of hope, and his
hope may live mith him as long as he liveth.
The hypocrites hope is nourished both with temporal and spi¬
ritual thinge. He hopeth that he hath the love and favour of
God, (because he enjoyeth many outuard (as he thinks) sa¬
vours from God. His estate is good here, and therefore he hopes
will be so hereafter. PPossibly he is rich, and great, and pro¬
sperous in the world, and thence concludeth, Surely God loves
me. Yes, and in reference to spirituals, the hypocrite may have
hope, he may be planted into Church-Priviledges, he may be
reckoned among Saints, or true believers; he may enjoy all the
Ordinances of the Gospel; he may eat bread at the Table of the
Lord, and fit among the Lords people; All which may breed
in him a great deal ot hope.
Further, He may have many and great spiritual gifts, yea,
he may have a fair appearance of grace; As he osten hath great
gifts of knowledge, of utterance, of prayer, so he may have that
which looks like grace, like faith, like repentance and godly sor¬
row, he may have that which looks like love and humility, and
patience, he may have the appearmces of all these graces, and
these may wind up his hope very high, and fill his sayls with such
strong confidences, that he may reckon himself among the dar¬
lings of heaven, and the delight of Christ. He may look upon
himfelf, not only as in favour uith God, but as one of Gods fa¬
vourites, and say in his heart, surely I shall be saved if any are to
be saved; he may come and lean upon the Lord, as the Prophet
tells us that sinful people did (Mic. 3.11.) The heads therefore
Judge for remard, and the Priests thereof teach for bire, and the Pro¬

say, is not the Lord among us, none evil can come upon us ? But in¬

saith, Egypt did to the house of Israel, uhen they took hold of thee

body.t: Secondly, Observe;
Death puts an hypocrite quite off from all his hope; when God
taketh amay his soul, bis hopeis also tak en axaf.
When he dyes, then all his fiopes dye; as when the Princes of
the world dye, their thoughts perish, so when they who are meer
worldlings perish, their hopes perish too. How can an hypocrite
hope for good in death, when his hope never enteted, nor ancho¬
red within the vail, for life? his hope is not fastened upon the
word of eternal life, and therefore his hope cannot be a stiy to his
soul when he departs this life. The hope that holds out is entred
into that within the vail (Heb. 6. 19.) chat is, it closeth with
God himself in Jesus Christ, it hath sweet Communion with
God by Jesus Christ our high Priest, who is our forerunuer is for
us entred into heaven. A beleever is subject to be tossed with
troubles of mind and manifold temptations, as a Ship upon the
Sea, while he is in this world; yet that hope which is entred
within the vaile, stayes him as an anchor sure and stedfist in all
stormes, and in all times. But the Anchor of the hypocrites hope
enters not within the vail, but is cast upon false and loose ground,
and therefore when the storme comes his anchor drives, and
unstedfast, and sohis hope and heart fail together. The stoutest
hypocrite in the world will droop at last, when God comes to
take away his soul; then his crest falls, and his Plumes sligge.
When the rain descendeth, and the floods come, and the miuds blow,
and beat upon the house that is built upon the sand, it falls, and tbe
fallthereof is great (Math. 7. 27.) A salse heart cannot hold out
in real hardships; when rain and floods and winds (by which are
meant all the troubles of this life ) assault him, he runs to ruine,
and cannot stand his ground : much lesse will he be able to stand
in the hour of death, when the raine and floods and winds
temptations fall most furiously upon the soul. Thus Solomon con¬
cludes (Prov.11. 7.) When a wiched man dyeth, his expectation
shall perish, and the hope of unjust men perisheth. Possibly that may
be everlisting which they hope for, yet their hopes are not lasting;
the hopes of some perish, because they hope only for perishing
things; others hive hopes of unperishing things, whose hope yst
shall perish. The voluptuous rich man is said to have had his good
1bings (Luke 16. 13.) he had no more to hope for, no more to

0089.head: Chip.27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOB. Vers,8.

body.t: looke for, his hope perisheth when God tooke away his soule.
When a godly man dyeth, his hope is perfected by the fruition
of that which he hoped for, he enjoyeth all and more than ever
he expected. But when an ungodly man dyeth, his hope perisheth
ina disappoyutment of fruition, he enjoyeth nothing at all of all
that, which he (though with litrle reason) so much expected.
Againe, I'hat is the hope of the hypocrite, though he have gai¬
ned? The Spirit of God joynes gaine with the hypocrite.
Hence Observe, Thirdly;
Covetousnesse and bypocrisie usually dwell together.
The true love of morldly gaine, and the false love of spirituall
gaine, hunt in couples, and are seldom severed. Hypocrisie aimes
at gaine, and often hits it, but it alwayes misseth true gaine;
falsenesse in the things of God, wvaites for fullness in the things of
men, but real fullness it gets none. When a false heart seeth that
religion is in credit, that godlyness is the wiy to worldly greatness
and that (as sometimes it doth, though rarely) che profession
it leadeth to advancement, presently he takes upon him the pro¬
fession of Religion, and puts onthe garbe or fashion of godlynesse.
Christ saith of hypocrites, They devoure widomes houses, and for
pretence mabe long prayers. A false heart prayeth, and will be much
duty, that he may devoure the houses and estates of others,
or that he may smooth his way to his own ends; but he cares not
tobe, nor is he at all in duty to draw neare to God, or improve
his own spiritual estate to the end. This is a dangerous temptati¬
on in these times, because now religion is look'd upon with a good
eye, and religious godly menare in place; a false heart works up¬
on this, and will be in any forme of religion, that hath a faire ac¬
ceptance in the world, through the favourable eye of Princes and
earthly Powers, cast uponit. The Apostle speakes of some (1Tim.
6.5.) who fupposed that gain was godlynefs; and surely the end
which such had in professing godlynesse, wis that they might be

counted godlynesse, which to their nitural appetite was bitter,
or atbest had no better tast in their palates, thin the white of an

Fourthly, Tob supposeth the hypocrite gaining.
Hence Note;
Hypocrites may, and usually do, gain much in this world.
As they have a great desire of worldly gain, so they get it;

mally spring out of the belly and bowels of the earth. The Lord

portion (which is all their portion) in this life. For as they are
but common professors, so these are but common mercies, such
as many òf his Enemies receive, who ire but fatted as Oxen for
the slaughter, and fitted for destraction. True happinesse is not

narrow bound: unlesse we get beyond the creature, and set our

fire, so they attain much of the world, but they shall attain no

Observe, Fifthly;
Riches or morldly gains avail nothing in the approaches

The hypocrite (which Job, Chap. 31. 24. professed he hid

body.t: comfort. The Apostle Paul could siy upon a well-grounded assu¬

Godlinesse will stand by us when we dye, the riches of faith, the

body.t: Christ, who knew the worth of a soul, and haid down a prlce to

What is a man profited if he shall gain the whole world, and lose bis

I, he is not at all profited by all the profits of the world, if he

Secondly, From those words, when God tabeth amay his
saule,
Observe;
The soul is at Gods dispose, he may send for it nhen he will.
The Lord can command iway the soul of the strongest, of the
richest, ot the wisest; Life and death are in the hand ot God. He
can either cut the thread of life, or spin it out at pleasure. Moses
tells the Jewes as one man (Deut.30.20.) He is thy life, and the
lengthof thy dayes. He also dispenceth death, and shortness of dayes.
The marriage of the soul and body together is life; the break¬
ing of this marrige bond, or the parting of soul and body
deith. God can part the soul from the body, he can break that
martiage bond when & how he pleaseth. He can uncloath the soul,
and leave it naked, he can quickly stripit of this garment of flesh.
The soul separate from the body is naked and uncloathed. So the
Apostle speiks about his own deith (2 Cor. 5.2, 3, 4.) Not
that be mould be uncloatbed, but eloathed upon, that mortality migbt
suallomid up of life. When ve are uncloathed or dye, mortali¬
swalloweth us up, but when we shall be cloathed upon with, or
live in glory, mortality shill be swallowed up. Now, as the time
when the body shall be cloathed with glory, and mortalit y shall be

body.t: Though hypocrites and most micked min dye a natural death?
pet to them their deathis violent.
Their souls are, as it were, snatcht and taken, yea rent and
torne fromthem, a wicked man doth not commend his soul into
the hands of God, but the hand of God taketh and pulleth his
soule from him. Old Simeon could say, Lord, now lettest thou thy
servant depart ix peace (Luke 2.29.) And Paul could say, I de¬
fire to depart (Phil. 1. 23.) No hypocrite could ever make auy
of these prayers, for if his tongue hath spoken them, his heart hath
not. An hypocrite may somtimes desire to dye, but he is never
willing to dye. We read in the book of the Revelation (Chap.9.
6.) that many men shall seck death, and shall not find it, and shall
desire to dye, and death shall flee from them. But was this because
they were willing to dye?no, but because they were weary of their
lives, or afraid to live: they did not see any other good in death,
but to get out of the pænal evils of this life. Thus a wicked man
miy desire to dye, that he may be quit of the troubles, miïeries,
and dangers that threaten his life; but he is never willing to dye
when he quietly enjoys the good things of this life; much lesse
doth he see thit the best things of this life are better’d in the next.
He doth not see that there is more good ro come than any that
he leaves; yez, he will not leave his sin, his beloved lust, for any
good that is to come. And therefore though the Lord suffer him
live till he be as fruit sully ripe, yea almost rotten, and ready
drop off the tree, though he be so old that he can live a natu¬
ral life no longer; yet his death is violent tohim. As the second
or eternal death rejoyns and reunites his soul to his body sore
against his will, so the first or temporal death separates and pulls
his soul from his body sore against his will. There are two spe¬
cial considerations, upon which it doth appeare, that a hypocrite
can never dye (in this sence) but a violent death.
Fitst, He cannot freely submit to the decree of deith; he
caunot dye in obedience as a true beleever doth. He that doth not
live in obedience, can never dye in obedience. As Christ was obedi¬
ent anto death, eventhe death of the Crosse; So Saints (in their de¬
gree) are obedient, not only all their lives, but they are obedient
unto death, that is, their dying is an act of obedience. But it
impossible that the bypocrite, mho never lived in obedience to

0094.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOB. Verf.8.

body.t: the commandment of God, should dye in obedience to the de¬
cree of God.
Secondly, He hath no footing in, or assurance of a better
life; he never took hold of eternil life, theresore he can never
willingly let go his hold of a temporal life. No man willingly
parts with what he hath, until he hath some evidence and assu¬
rance, at least some good hope of that which is better; or which
he (at least ) conceives to be better than whit he hath. A min
will not readily give up his possession of a smoaky Cottage, when
he sees, if he leave it, he must be exposed to all the injuries of wind
and weather, of frost and snow, in the open aire. So then, He
that hath not in him a principle of obedience, while he lives, nor
well-grounded hope of happiness when he dyeth, cannot dye wil¬
lingly. And therefore, that is verified upon every wicked man in
the world when he dyeth, which is said to the worldly rich man,
Lube 12. 20.) This night shall thy soul be required of thee: His
foul is required, not refigned, tis taken away, not given up; and
though he say, he desireth to be dissolved, yet to be dissolved
none of his desire; He may choose death (according to his cor¬
rupt Judgment) as the lesser evel, but he never chooseth it as
that which leadeth to the greatest good.
Thus we have seen somewhat of Jobs mind in asserting the
sincerity of his foul towards God, by his hope in God when his
foul should leave his body, while he in ’a way of diminution puts
the question, n'hat is the hope of the hypocrité, though he hath gai¬
ned, nhen God tatetb amay his sout ?

body.t: JOB, Chap. 27. verf. 9, 10.
Will God heare bis cry, mhen trouble cometh upon him?
will he delight himself in theAlmighty? mill he alwayes

Eserted in the former verse, that, The hypocrite hatb no hope;

He that hath hope shill be answered when he prayeth, God will

The sence of the questionis Negative; He will not, and therefore

body.t: uben trouble cometh.
The action or motion of a living creature is here ascribed to

person or an army. Thus it is expressed by Solomon ( Pro. 6. 11.)
So shall thy poverty comt as ons that travelletb, and thy want as an

armed man, because it comes violently, and as to him irresistably.
Thus trouble cometh upon the hypocrite, it cometh like an armed

body.t: Now the troubles thit come upon the hypocrite, are of two

And he that did ever pray (I do not say, he that ever said

Adoptiòn, That man cannot but (in the sence explained ) be al¬

Secondly, From the words considered in themselves, note;
At is our duty to call upon God alwayes.
The text implies this clearly, other texts speak it plainly.
The Lord gives a Parable ( Luke 18.) and this is the scope of it,
(v. 1.) He spake a Parable unto them, to this end, that men ought

Pray mithout ceasing, (1 Thess.5. 17.) (There are many urgent

First, We cannot subsist a minute without the assistince of
God; for in him me live and move, and have our being, (Acts 17.
28.) And as we hive our life, motion, and being, so the comforts
of our life, the guidance of our motions, and our well-being from
him. Therefore we must alwayes pray, both to acknowledge
our dependance, and to receive assistance from him.
Secondly, We are continually besieged with evils and temp¬
tations, we have enemies about us, either visible or invisible,
seen or unseen, therefore we have need to pray continually.
we had enemies alwayes in sight we vould pray alwayes, we have
unseene enemies alwayes abour us, and these are the most dange¬
rous enemies, therefore we have more need alwayes to pray, and
Thirdly,
call in the aide of God against them.

0118.head: Chap.27. An Exposition apon the Book of IOR. Verf.ic.

body.t: Thirdly, We have work to do continually; & we know our
duty, we can never be out of work; and what-ever we do¬

Fourthly, We are centinually using the creature, we use

As every creature of God is good (init self) soit is sanctified (unto

Fisthly, We are often in troubles and afflictions. Now the

Sixthly, When we are at ease and quiet, in health and peace,

Seventhly, We sin continually, ve sin (is I may say) with¬

Eighthly, We ought continually to glorifie God, therefore

ciency to do whit we asl, and his goodnesse in being alwayes

Yet this poynt is not so to be understood, as if we should doe

Thirdly, Observe, (which is implyed in the Question, mul he

A bypocrite vill not almayes call upon God.
You may see him set out very full of metdle; he sets out about

First, When he speeds not in prayer, then he will throw up

or when God seemes in his providence to speak contrary to his

no desire to duty when he cannot get what he desires by duty.
It is with him as with some drast Horses, they will draw when the

body.t: Secondly, Take the contrary; If the hypõctite speed in pray¬

fore

From all, Tobs inferres, that he was no hypocrite; for though God

body.t: The general scope which Job drives at in this Chipter, is to
